question.explanation:
Let $u = 1 - 3x^2.$ Then \[ \dfrac{\textrm d u}{\textrm d x} = -6x \quad \Longrightarrow\quad \left(-\dfrac{1}{6}\right) \textrm d u= x \, \textrm d x, \] and we can solve the resulting integral as follows:

\begin{align*} \int \dfrac{x}{1 - 3x^2} \,\textrm d x & = \int\dfrac{1}{1 - 3x^2} \cdot x \,\textrm d x\\[5pt] & = \int\dfrac{1}{u} \cdot \left(-\dfrac{1}{6}\right) \textrm d u\\[5pt] & = -\dfrac{1}{6}\int\dfrac{1}{u} \,\textrm d u\\[5pt] & = -\dfrac{1}{6} \ln|u| + C\\[5pt] & = -\dfrac{1}{6} \ln\left|1 - 3x^2\right| + C \end{align*}

question.explanation:
In this case, the term $2x^5$ outside the parentheses isn't quite the derivative of $4+x^6.$ But the derivative is $6x^5,$ so we're only out by a constant factor. So we make the substitution $$ u = 4+x^6. $$ Its derivative is given by

\begin{align} \dfrac{\textrm{d}u}{\textrm{d}x} & = 6x^5\quad \Longrightarrow\quad\dfrac{1}{3}\textrm{d}u = 2x^5\,\textrm{d}x, \end{align}

and we can now write our integral in terms of $u,$ as follows:

\begin{align*} \int 2x^5(4+x^6)^{5}\,\textrm{d}x & =\int (4+x^6)^{5} \cdot 2x^5\,\textrm{d}x\\[5pt] & = \int u^{5} \cdot \dfrac{1}{3} \textrm d u\\[5pt] & = \dfrac{1}{3}\int u^{5} \, \textrm d u \end{align*}

Finally, we can solve the integral in terms of $u$ and then write the final result in terms of $x.$ We get

\begin{align*} \dfrac{1}{3} \int u^{5} \, \textrm d u & = \dfrac{1}{3}\cdot \dfrac{u^{6}}{6} + C\\[5pt] &= \dfrac{1}{18}u^{6} + C\\[5pt] &= \dfrac{1}{18}(4+x^6)^{6} + C\\[5pt] & = \dfrac{(4+x^6)^{6}}{18} + C. \end{align*}

example.title: Integrating an Expression Involving a Power Function Multiplied by a Constant Multiple of Its Derivative

question.explanation:
In this case, the term $9x^8$ outside the parentheses isn't quite the derivative of $9+2x^9.$ But the derivative is $18x^8,$ so we're only out by a constant factor. So we make the substitution $$ u = 9+2x^9. $$ Its derivative is given by

\begin{align} \dfrac{\textrm{d}u}{\textrm{d}x} & = 18x^8\quad \Longrightarrow\quad\dfrac{1}{2}\textrm{d}u = 9x^8\,\textrm{d}x, \end{align}

and we can now write our integral in terms of $u,$ as follows:

\begin{align*} \int 9x^8(9+2x^9)^{3}\,\textrm{d}x & =\int (9+2x^9)^{3} \cdot 9x^8\,\textrm{d}x\\[5pt] & = \int u^{3} \cdot \dfrac{1}{2} \textrm d u\\[5pt] & = \dfrac{1}{2}\int u^{3} \, \textrm d u \end{align*}

Finally, we can solve the integral in terms of $u$ and then write the final result in terms of $x.$ We get

\begin{align*} \dfrac{1}{2} \int u^{3} \, \textrm d u & = \dfrac{1}{2}\cdot \dfrac{u^{4}}{4} + C\\[5pt] &= \dfrac{1}{8}u^{4} + C\\[5pt] &= \dfrac{1}{8}(9+2x^9)^{4} + C\\[5pt] & = \dfrac{(9+2x^9)^{4}}{8} + C. \end{align*}
